planting.note: Divide and transplant bulb clumps in early fall into consistently moist to seasonally wet soil; seed is slow and benefits from several months of cold, moist stratification before it will germinate reliably.

directions: Pacific onion is a clump-forming wild allium native to wet mountain meadows, seeps, and streambanks of the western United States, and it is one of the few culinary onions that genuinely prefers damp feet rather than well-drained soil. Site it in a boggy or regularly irrigated spot with dappled shade from nearby trees or shrubs, mimicking the partial-shade woodland edges and subalpine meadows where it naturally grows. Established clumps can be divided every few years to control spacing and share plants, and both the broad flat leaves and the bulbs can be harvested and used fresh wherever a strong onion-garlic flavor is wanted. Because wild populations are slow to recover from overharvesting, take only a portion of any clump and allow the rest to regrow for next season.

planting.note: Transplant bulb divisions with roots intact in early fall into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil under deciduous shade; this variety is slower from seed than it is from divisions and colonies take several years to bulk up to a harvestable size.

directions: Narrow-leaf ramps are a distinct botanical variety of the familiar eastern ramp, recognized by narrower leaves, a whiter (less red-tinged) stem base, and an earlier emergence and die-back than the common broad-leaf form. It occupies the same rich, shaded hardwood-forest habitat as typical ramps but is less frequently harvested commercially, which makes it a worthwhile plant for a dedicated woodland food garden seeking to diversify beyond the more heavily foraged form. Grow it exactly as you would ramps: rich, moist, well-drained soil under a closed deciduous canopy, left largely undisturbed once established. Harvest sparingly, taking a portion of leaves or bulbs from a colony rather than clearing it, since regrowth from seed is very slow.

common_name: Grote Noordhollandse Mâche (Large Dutch Corn Salad)

planting.note: Direct-sow in early fall for a hardy overwintering crop, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable; this large-leaved Dutch heirloom tolerates light shade and short days better than most salad greens.

directions: This classic Dutch heirloom mâche produces notably larger, rounder rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves than standard corn salad, giving a bigger harvest per plant while keeping the same mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavor. Sow thickly in cool, moist, fertile soil in fall for overwintering under light mulch or a cold frame in colder zones, or in earliest spring; it grows well in the dappled shade of taller crops or deciduous trees, making it a useful filler for partially shaded beds during the short days of fall and early spring when little else will thrive. Keep soil consistently moist, since mâche bolts and turns bitter quickly in dry or hot conditions. Harvest whole rosettes or individual outer leaves once plants reach a usable size, and succession-sow every few weeks through the cool season for a continuous supply.

planting.note: Transplant rooted divisions or potted plants in spring into humus-rich soil in dappled shade; this low, spreading bramble roots readily from its creeping rhizomes and fills in as a groundcover within a couple of seasons.

directions: Strawberry raspberry is a low, herbaceous, nearly thornless Japanese bramble grown more as an ornamental groundcover than a serious fruit crop, spreading by creeping underground rhizomes to form a dense, ferny-leaved mat under open-canopy trees or along shaded woodland edges. It produces large, showy, puffy red berries shaped like oversized raspberries; the berries are edible and visually striking, though they are typically bland and seedy compared with true raspberries, so most gardeners grow it primarily for its tidy shade groundcover habit and ornamental fruit display. Plant it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade and let the rhizomes spread to fill the allotted space, trimming back the perimeter if it begins to wander into unwanted areas. It dies back to the ground each winter and resprouts reliably from the roots each spring.
